Paedo-communion
PEE-doh kuh-MYOON-yun
n. phrase (sacramental theology; the practice of admitting baptized infants and young children to the Lord's Supper prior to any formal profession of faith)
Paedo- from Greek pais (child, infant). Communion from Latin communio (sharing, fellowship), from communis (common). The compound term names the liturgical practice of extending the Lord's Supper to covenant children who have been baptized but have not yet made a credible profession of faith. It is distinct from credobaptist practice, which requires conversion before any sacramental participation, and from the majority paedobaptist position, which requires a credible profession before the Supper even when baptism was administered in infancy.

Biblical Definition

Paedo-communion is the position that covenant children who have received baptism as infants should also be admitted to the Lord's Supper without waiting for a formal profession of faith. Its primary argument is covenantal consistency: if covenant infants receive the initiatory sign (baptism) on the strength of their parents' faith and their membership in the covenant community, why should they be excluded from the covenant meal? Proponents cite the Passover typology (Exo 12:26; Deut 16:11, 14), in which children clearly participated in the Old Testament feast that the Lord's Supper fulfills. The Sinai covenant included children in its covenant meals (Exo 24:11); New Covenant exclusion of children from the New Covenant meal therefore requires positive warrant from the New Testament. Against paedo-communion, the classic Protestant and Reformed position reads 1 Corinthians 11:28 — “a man must examine himself” — as establishing a cognitive and moral self-examination prerequisite that infants and young children cannot perform. The judgment warning of 1 Corinthians 11:29 (“he who eats and drinks, eats and drinks judgment to himself if he does not judge the body rightly”) makes responsible discernment a prerequisite for participation. The 1689 LBCF (30.3–4) and Westminster Standards require that communicants “examine themselves as to their knowledge to discern the Lord's body, their faith to feed upon him, their repentance, love, and new obedience” — a standard that excludes non-professing infants by design.

Webster 1828 Definition

The sacramental practice of admitting baptized covenant infants and young children to the Lord's Supper prior to a credible profession of faith; argued on the basis of covenantal consistency with the Passover typology, but rejected by the Reformed and Baptist confessional standards on the basis of 1 Corinthians 11:28–29's self-examination requirement.

PAEDO-COMMUNION, n. phrase. The practice of admitting baptized children, including infants, to the Lord's Supper on the basis of their covenant membership rather than requiring a personal profession of faith and self-examination. The position is advocated within certain Reformed, Federal Vision, and sacramental-covenantal communities, and is the norm in Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism (which administers Communion only at the age of reason, but some Orthodox traditions give it to all the baptized from infancy).

The paedo-communion argument proceeds from the Passover typology: the Passover meal, which the Lord's Supper fulfills and replaces (Luke 22:19; 1 Cor 5:7), was a household feast from which children were not excluded. Exodus 12:26 assumes children will ask about it: “And it will come about when your children will say to you, 'What does this rite mean to you?'” Psalm 78:4 demonstrates that covenant children were included in the covenant community's memorial celebration: “We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD.” If the type included children, the argument runs, the antitype should not exclude them.

The classical Reformed and Baptist response is grounded in 1 Corinthians 11:27–32: Paul's warning that eating and drinking “in an unworthy manner” incurs judgment, combined with the command to “examine himself” before participating, establishes a cognitive and moral prerequisite that infants and non-professing young children cannot fulfill. The self-examination of verse 28 is not mere ritual; it requires faith, repentance, discernment of the Lord's body, and gratitude — capacities that require regenerate understanding. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 171–175) and the 1689 LBCF (30.3–4) codify this requirement.

The Federal Vision movement (Auburn Avenue Theology, Norman Shepherd, Peter Leithart) incorporated paedo-communion as a corollary of its covenantal theology, arguing that baptism confers a “real but resistible” covenant grace that entitles the baptized to full sacramental participation. This view was censured by multiple Reformed denominations (PCA, OPC, URCNA) as incompatible with the Westminster Standards' doctrine of saving grace and the nature of the Lord's Supper.

The majority confessional Reformed and Baptist position is that the Lord's Supper requires a credible profession of faith, demonstrated repentance, and the ability to self-examine — a standard that children reach at the age of a genuine profession, however young that may be. Early profession with genuine evidences is not delayed; it is welcomed. Perpetual exclusion of professing children is not the standard; non-professing children are not yet ready for the Table.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 11:28 — "But a man must examine himself — and in so doing he is to eat of the bread and drink of the cup."

1 Corinthians 11:29 — "For he who eats and drinks, eats and drinks judgment to himself if he does not judge the body rightly."

Luke 22:19 — "And when He had taken some bread and given thanks, He broke it, and gave it to them, saying, “This is My body which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of Me.”"

Psalm 78:4 — "We will not hide them from their children, Telling to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, And His strength and His wonderful works that He has done."

Modern Corruption

The Federal Vision movement embedded paedo-communion within a covenantal framework that blurred the distinction between external covenant membership and saving grace, producing a sacramentalism that multiple Reformed assemblies formally censured; Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic practice admits infants without the self-examination 1 Corinthians 11 requires.

expand to see more

The Federal Vision (FV) theology that emerged from the 2002 Auburn Avenue Pastor's Conference (Doug Wilson, Steve Wilkins, Peter Leithart, John Barach) incorporated paedo-communion as a natural extension of its covenantalism. If baptism objectively grafts the infant into Christ and confers real covenant benefits, then exclusion from the Supper is arbitrary. The FV position, however, was censured not merely for paedo-communion but for the broader theological framework: its account of baptismal regeneration, covenantal election, and resistible covenant grace was found by the PCA, OPC, and URCNA to be incompatible with the Westminster Standards' distinction between the outward administration of the covenant and saving grace. Paedo-communion was the visible tip of an iceberg of covenantal revisionism.

Eastern Orthodox and some Roman Catholic practice (the Orthodox administer the chalice to infants from baptism) argue from patristic precedent and sacramental theology that the baptized belong fully to the Eucharistic body. This position is consistent within a sacramental-regeneration framework — but it is precisely that framework that Reformed and Baptist theology rejects. The Westminster Standards and 1689 LBCF require self-examination (1 Cor 11:28) as a prerequisite, not as a post-hoc ratification; the Supper's benefits are received by faith, not by membership in the visible community. Admitting those who cannot examine themselves or exercise faith — even covenant infants — gives the sign without the reality and risks the judgment Paul warns of in 1 Corinthians 11:30.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The paedo-communion debate is rooted in the typological relationship between Passover and the Lord's Supper, the Pauline self-examination requirement of 1 Corinthians 11, the Federal Vision controversy of 2002–2010, and the historic Reformed confessional standards on the Lord's Supper.

expand to see more

Passover typology (Exo 12; Luke 22:19; 1 Cor 5:7) — the Lord's Supper as the fulfillment of Passover; paedo-communionists argue that children participated in the Passover and should therefore participate in the Supper; the counterargument is that the New Covenant adds the self-examination requirement of 1 Cor 11:28.

1 Corinthians 11:17–34 — the Pauline foundation for the Lord's Supper as a covenant meal requiring genuine faith, self-examination, and discernment of the Lord's body; the warning of verse 29 establishes a cognitive and moral prerequisite that defines who may rightly participate.

Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 171–175 / 1689 LBCF 30.3–4 — the confessional standards for communicant preparation: knowledge to discern the Lord's body, faith to feed on Christ, repentance, love, and new obedience; a standard that excludes non-professing infants by explicit design.

Federal Vision controversy (2002–2010) — PCA, OPC, and URCNA reports on Federal Vision theology, all of which found its covenantalism and paedo-communion incompatible with the Westminster Standards; the controversy sharpened the confessional Reformed position on Supper prerequisites.

Eastern Orthodox practice — communion from infancy administered immediately after baptism and chrismation; the most ancient and consistent example of paedo-communion in practice; its framework of sacramental regeneration makes paedo-communion internally coherent in ways that are unavailable to Reformed covenantalism.

Usage

"The paedo-communion debate is not primarily about children's feelings or inclusion; it is about the nature of the Lord's Supper — whether it is a covenant meal received by faith alone, or a covenant meal received by membership in the covenant community; the self-examination texts of 1 Corinthians 11 provide the decisive answer."

"A church that welcomes professing children to the Table at a young age (with genuine evidences of faith and understanding) is not practicing paedo-communion; paedo-communion specifically means admission before any credible profession, on the basis of baptism alone."

"Pastors serving in paedobaptist traditions should teach their congregations clearly why the Standards require self-examination before communion and why this standard applies to baptized children awaiting profession — the goal is not gatekeeping but protecting the communicant from eating and drinking judgment (1 Cor 11:29)."
